runs.text: Trocar o amor, ou amar mais hũa

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's verb example with yuru. The Portuguese defines transferring one's love or loving one thing more than another; the scan reads Trocar, not OCR Trocor.
Completes the comparison between two objects of love. Iennintachiua begins the example about the saints, while xeca- continues as xecai on the next row.

Xecaiuo Deus ni voboximexi cayerareta describes preferring God to the world. The honorific form has the saints as its acting subject; Deus remains the printed Latin/Portuguese divine name inside the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Sanctos amarão mais a Deos, que ao mundo.

lines.note: The Portuguese translation explicitly says that the saints loved God more than the world, fixing the comparison in the preceding Japanese example.
Oboshimeshi-ire is glossed as loving someone greatly. The printed principal parts uru and eta belong to the compound verb and are not modernized.
Oboye denotes memory. The example begins oboye no tsuyoi hito, literally a person whose memory is strong, with tsuyoi divided across the row boundary.
Yoi completes tsuyoi, and hito supplies the person described as having a good memory. This is a continuation of the preceding example.
The second oboye means reputation or fame, and oboye wo toru means acquiring it. Fama is visibly upright in this impression and is retained in that typeface despite being Portuguese.
Brar completes the divided Portuguese cobrar: acquiring a name and reputation. The short line closes the fame sense of oboye.
The verb oboye is first glossed as feeling or perceiving. Mi no ita- begins the bodily-pain example, whose noun continues on the next row.
Itami wo oboyuru means feeling bodily pain; the Portuguese sentir dores do corpo confirms that reading. The historical uru form is retained.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Lembrarſe, ou ter na memoria. Vt,

lines.note: The next sense is remembering or holding something in memory. The roman O- at the right edge begins Oratio in the Japanese example below, rather than belonging to the italic Portuguese gloss.
Completes Oratio wo oboyetaka: have you learned the prayers by heart? The Portuguese question confirms memorization, rather than mere familiarity with the prayers.
Oobuku is a large serving of tea. The gloss literally gives a large occasion or round of tea, and the headword retains the printed circumflex.
Oobukuro means a large bag, directly matched by grande saco. The long initial vowel distinguishes the compound from the following short-vowel obuto.
Ooburumai is a grand feast or entertainment. Grande conuite describes the scale of the hospitality, without requiring modernization of the historical spelling.

runs.text: Çapatos feitos de junco que tem o ca

lines.note: Obuto names rush sandals with a thick fastening. The capital in Çapatos has a visible cedilla; ca begins cabrestilho on the following physical row without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: breſtilho großo, que ſe mete entre os dedos.

lines.note: Completes cabrestilho and explains the thick thong placed between the toes. The Portuguese description identifies the footwear rather than an independent sense of the headword.
Ooka is explained through uta as songs or verses. The final upright S. labels written usage; it is separated from the italic gloss.
Oka is a small treeless hill or mound. The lack of a long-vowel mark distinguishes it from the neighboring oo- compounds.
Ookaze is a great wind or storm. The gloss confirms the weather meaning; the Jesuit je spelling corresponds to the voiced syllable in kaze.

The wolf-name is visibly printed Vôcame, with final e. It is retained as printed rather than silently changed to the familiar modern ookami. The subsequently consulted supplied NINJAL index also lists Vôcame (NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, v202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); the scan remains the transcription authority.
Okami denotes a horse's tail and mane. Vo- starts the repeated headword in the following example, and the Portuguese coma is retained as the printed word for mane.
Okami wo kitte hanasu means releasing a horse after cutting its tail and mane. Enlargement shows two t types in qitte, correcting OCR qite; the gloss continues on the next row.
Completes the horse example: after cutting the tail and mane, let the horse go. Soltalo supplies the action expressed by hanasu.
Oka no be denotes upland open ground, hills, or fields. The Portuguese begins a fuller description of the uncultivated terrain on the next row.

runs.text: que ſe não lauram, nem tẽ aruoredos, ou mato.

lines.note: The land is neither cultivated nor covered with trees or scrub. The abbreviated tẽ is retained without expanding the nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: Nora, ou Camiſama moça que ain-

lines.note: Okata describes a daughter-in-law or young Camiſama who has not yet assumed control of the house. Camiſama occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: da não tem tomado poße da caſa.

lines.note: Completes the qualification that the woman has not yet taken possession of the house. Poße is the printed double-s form, not an invitation to normalize its spelling.
Okatadono, equated with Taifo, denotes a widow. The following row narrows this to the widow of a lord; Taifo is preserved as the visible form.

runs.text: q̃ foi de algũ Tono ja viuua. No

lines.note: The widow was the wife of a Tono; the entry then states the regional designation used in Ximo. Both Japanese terms occur within Portuguese prose and are marked for whole-word typeface review.
Xinpǒ completes the Portuguese statement giving the Ximo regional name for the widow. The visible caron is retained, and the term is marked because it belongs to that explanatory sentence.
Ookata first means for the greater part. The second item repeats the word for an ordinary or moderate thing, beginning across the row break.
Completes the repeated ookata and gives the attributive alternative ookatano. The scan has a comma after cata; the gloss continues as ordinaria below.
Dinaria completes ordinaria. Kore ookatano koto dewa begins an example asserting that this is no ordinary matter, with the negative on the next row.

runs.text: Iſto não he qualquer couſa, nem das or-

lines.note: Nai completes the negative Japanese sentence. The Portuguese says this is not just any thing or one of the ordinary things, preserving the divided or- at the edge.
Dinarias completes ordinarias, closing the explanation that the matter is out of the ordinary. The row is a genuine continuation despite its brevity.
Okashi, okasu, okashita means committing or doing something, particularly a crime or sin in this sense. The visible cri- corrects OCR eri- before me below.
Completes crime and introduces toga wo okasu, committing an offense. Peccado and the example establish the moral or criminal sense of okasu.
The Portuguese reads peccado, not OCR paccado. Tano me wo okasu introduces a second example concerning another man's wife.
The translation describes adultery with another man's wife. Yamaini then begins the passive example in which illness afflicts someone.
Yamai ni okasaruru means being afflicted by illness. The Portuguese gives becoming ill or being badly treated by the disease, completed below.

runs.text: da doença. ¶ Item, Zombar, ou enga-

lines.note: Da doença completes the illness gloss. The next sense is mocking or deceiving, with enganar divided at the physical line end.
Kimi wo okasu means mocking or deceiving one's lord in this context. The visibly separated Zom bar is retained as printed rather than joined silently.
Completes the reference to the lord and introduces tengu ni okasaruru. Tengu is the agent in a Japanese example, not a term embedded in the Portuguese gloss.
Saruru completes the passive verb. The Portuguese offers being mocked, deceived, or tempted; ten- continues on the next row.
Tado completes tentado, and do demonio gives the dictionary's Christian rendering of the tengu as a demon. The line closes this entry before the next column.

zones.label: Column 2 running header
zones.note: The scan prints an anomalous initial T in this V-before-O running header; it is retained rather than regularized.

lines.note: Okashi is explained by okasu koto, the act of committing an offense. The gloss begins with committing a crime and continues with the fault or sin itself.

runs.text: falta, ou o peccado, ou crime.

lines.note: Completes the noun definition as a fault, sin, or crime. This row remains distinct from the following adjective okashii, which has a different meaning.
Okashii denotes something laughable or ridiculous. The double final ij is the printed adjectival ending and should not be reduced.
Okashisa is the corresponding noun for the quality of being amusing or ridiculous. The indented short row belongs with the adjective above.
Okashuu is the adverbial form, explicitly labeled Aduer. The caron on u is visible and retained as a length mark.
Okashiubai combines deception or affront with taking something away. Enlargement supports enga- before nando below, correcting OCR enge- while retaining the printed carons in the verb forms.

runs.text: nando ao ſenhor, ou outra peßoa alta tomar per

lines.note: Completes enganando and names the lord or another high-ranking person as the person deceived. Tomar per begins the explanation of forcible seizure.
Força completes per força: taking something by force. The tilde on algũa is retained over u as printed.
Okkake means running after or pursuing someone. The principal forms preserve the historical uru conjugation supplied by the dictionary.
Ir lhe no alcance completes the pursuit gloss, literally going after someone to catch up. It belongs to okkake rather than the following scattering verb.
Occhiraxi describes scattering or routing, especially enemies. The Portuguese expression eſpalha fato retains its printed separation, and co- begins como on the next row.
The enemies provide the example of what is scattered. Teki wo voc- begins the Japanese example, whose verb continues as vocchirasu below.
Chirasu completes vocchirasu in the example of routing the enemy. This short continuation preserves the physical split of the verb.
Okkomi means putting something inside, shutting it in, or surrounding it. The supplied past form ôda retains its visible circumflex.
Cerrar completes encerrar; cercar adds surrounding or enclosing. Hito wo okkomu illustrates shutting a person inside.

runs.text: Meter alguem dentro dalgũa caſa, ou encerra.

lines.note: The example is rendered as putting someone into a house or shutting him in. The final printed mark after encerra is retained provisionally as the OCR period; lo follows on the next row.
Lo completes the preceding verb-plus-pronoun construction, with como preſo specifying confinement like a prisoner. The short physical continuation is retained.
Okkudaxi means throwing something forcefully from above to below. The Japanese aita is a historical past form, and ri- begins Portuguese riba.

runs.text: ba pera baixo, ou fazer decer.

lines.note: Ba completes riba, and the remainder gives downward motion or making something descend. Decer is preserved as the historical printed spelling.
Okkuzuxi is destroying or breaking up an enemy while pursuing them. The gloss ties the action to the chase, and alcãce retains its nasal abbreviation.
Oochakuna is glossed as showing arrogance or liking ostentation. The definition should not be replaced with the common modern sense of being lazy or shirking.
De fausto completes the reference to liking pomp or display. The source's st typography is retained without a global long-s substitution.
Ochi, alternatively ochi no hito, denotes a nurse who suckles a child. The Portuguese ama que cria provides the functional identification.
The long-vowel oochi is simply identified as a tree of that name. The short gloss does not itself warrant adding a botanical species identification.
Ochi, otsuru, ochita is the verb to fall from a height. Co- begins konomi, the fruit in the first example below.
Konomi ga otsuru describes fruit falling from a tree. The Portuguese fruita is retained as printed rather than normalized to fruta.
Toga ni otsuru extends falling to committing a sin. The Portuguese cair em peccado supplies the figurative sense explicitly.
Sono hito ni ochita is explained as consenting with that person. The rest of the translation below specifies joining that person in wrongdoing.

runs.text: homem, ou com eßa peßoa caindo com ellaem

lines.note: Completes the reference to that man or person and begins the phrase falling with that person into sin. The scan supports final m in the tightly set ellaem, correcting OCR ellaen without inserting an unsupported space.
After completing the sin example, shiro ga otsuru means that a fortress falls or surrenders. The damaged r in Xiroga and the Portuguese Render- are supported by enlargement and the fortress context.
Se a fortaleza completes render-se, the surrender of the fortress. Shukke wo otsuru introduces abandoning the religious life; the edge prints Dei without a secure hyphen before xar below.

runs.text: xar a religião, & fazerſe ſecular. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Xar completes deixar: leaving religion and becoming secular. The margin abbreviation is Itẽ, with a visible nasal mark, not OCR lli.

runs.text: Fugir, ou acolherſe vencido na guerra. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Another sense is fleeing or taking refuge after defeat in war. The repeated marginal Itẽ introduces the following confession sense.

runs.text: Confeßar o reo, ou o que

lines.note: Vochi tçuru introduces confession by an accused person or someone subjected to tratos. The source leaves the two Japanese forms separated by a space without supplying an editorial comma.
The person tells the truth under interrogation or torture. Tôniua vochi- begins the contrast between being questioned and revealing something while talking.

Ide completes vochiide in the negative first half: not confessing when questioned. Cataruni votçuru contrasts confessing while talking; the following Portuguese calou confirms the silence under questioning.

runs.text: calou, & em pratica ſem tratos confeßou.

lines.note: When questioned, the person kept silent, but confessed in conversation without tratos. This completes the contrast in the Japanese expression rather than describing two separate speakers.
Ochi, preferably kami no ochi, is fallen hair. The Latin potiùs indicates the preferred fuller expression; the Portuguese cabelos is divided across the row break.

runs.text: los que caem da cabeça das molheres de que fa-

lines.note: Los completes cabelos: hair shed from women's heads. The line begins explaining what is subsequently made from it, with fa- continuing below.
Zem completes fazem, and the fallen hair is made into wigs. Postiças retains the locally printed st reading without generalizing its ligature classification.
Oochi is equated with ookina michi, a large road, and glossed as a public road. The scan reads publica, correcting OCR publiu, and shows a comma after i.

runs.text: como caminho que vai pera o Miyaco.

lines.note: The road leading to the Miyaco is the example of a public thoroughfare. Miyaco occurs inside a Portuguese sentence and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Lugar onde as agoas que correm de

lines.note: Ochiai denotes the place where streams coming from different directions meet. The definition continues its description of the confluence below.
The waters from different places meet there. Ochiai- begins the example ochiai no mizzu, preserving the printed line-end mark.
No mizzu completes the example: the water of a confluence. The doubled zz is retained as the dictionary's spelling.

The verb ochiai means waters meeting together. The visible em corrects OCR en; the printed Encontrarenſe is retained without modernizing its consonants. The last principal part is followed by a visible comma, not a period.

runs.text: algum lugar. ¶ Item, Encontrarenſe os que

lines.note: Completes the sense of waters meeting in some place and starts another sense about people meeting. The scan supports algum lugar and Encontrarenſe os que, replacing the garbled OCR; the following word is supplied only as the separate catchword.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The bottom-right word is the printed catchword vão. Its reading is taken from this page; the following page is not supplied.
